solutions.check: 30 entries; each light the paper's grid did not give solved here from its clue's wordplay (an anagram or hidden word, the one listed word fitting every crossing) and its definition (WordNet), as the answer another puzzle gave the same clue, or as the one past answer its crossings left that the printed letters allow, agrees with the 29 answers the paper printed

clue.text: Stormy Atlantic is one scourge of sailors

indicators.note: a stormy sea is tossed about, so the letters of these three words are churned into a new order

explanation.surface: A rough Atlantic is one of the things sailors dread most.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stormy' is the anagram signal, rearranging ATLANTICISONE; the surface makes the stormy ocean itself the scourge.
explanation.definitionFit: The knotted whip of nine cords was the notorious naval punishment, a literal scourge for flogging seamen.

clue.text: Keeps in a highly dry place? Fancy!

parts.note: a keep is a castle's central tower, so keeps are castles
taken as written
the rain in Spain falls mainly on the plain, leaving the highlands dry

explanation.surface: Fortresses on some arid plateau: what a fanciful notion!
explanation.walkthrough: The highlands of Spain are dry because, as the song says, its rain falls mainly on the plain.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names daydreams and impossible schemes, a pure fancy with no foundation.

clue.text: Having an irregular nap, in imperial style

definitions.meaning: fabric with its pile in clumps rather than smooth
an imperial is a small pointed beard, a tuft below the lower lip

explanation.surface: A rug with an uneven pile, styled like an emperor's.
explanation.walkthrough: An imperial is a small chin beard, named after Napoleon III.
explanation.definitionFit: Tufts are clumps, whether of fabric pile or of the chin hair called an imperial beard.

clue.text: Healer takes a turn for the worse at Ringway

indicators.note: taking a turn for the worse suggests a change in shape, so the letters of a turn are rearranged

parts.note: a ring is O for its shape and a way is a path

explanation.surface: A healer falls ill at Ringway, the old name for Manchester's airport.
explanation.walkthrough: Ringway is Manchester airport, which hides ring (O) plus way (PATH); 'for the worse' reshuffles A TURN to NATUR.
explanation.definitionFit: Practitioners of nature cure treat illness with diet and natural remedies rather than drugs.

clue.text: Well-instructed in New Latin about the wedding

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other
new suggests the word Latin is made afresh, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: to be well up in a subject is to know it thoroughly

explanation.surface: A scholar well versed in modern Latin writes about the wedding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' reads as part of the phrase New Latin, but it is the anagram signal; 'about the wedding' is the definition, not a container.
explanation.definitionFit: Matters relating to marriage ceremonies are described by this adjective, as in the vows of a bride and groom.

clue.text: Punch line for him was dropping the pilot

definitions.text: Punch line for him was dropping the pilot

parts.words: Punch line for him was dropping the pilot
parts.note: the cartoonist of the magazine Punch whose famous drawing 'Dropping the Pilot' showed Bismarck leaving the ship of state

explanation.surface: For some comedian, the joke's punchline involved dumping the pilot.
explanation.walkthrough: Punch was the British humour magazine; 'Dropping the Pilot' (1890) is its most famous cartoon, showing Bismarck dismissed by the Kaiser. 'Punch line' means the drawn line in Punch.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir John, chief cartoonist of Punch and Alice illustrator, drew the celebrated Bismarck cartoon of 1890.

clue.text: Holly is one above the law

indicators.note: in a down entry one piece placed above another comes first

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
lex is Latin for law

explanation.surface: Holly believes she is above the law.
explanation.walkthrough: Holly reads as a woman's name but is the plant; ilex is its botanical genus.
explanation.definitionFit: The holly genus carries this Latin botanical name.

clue.text: But don't expect it to have a cube root!

definitions.text: But don't expect it to have a cube root!

parts.words: But don't expect it to have a cube root!
parts.note: a crop that is a root and is made into sweetener, though no lumps grow on it

explanation.surface: A maths teacher warns that this number will not have a cube root.
explanation.walkthrough: Cube root is a maths term, but here it is a root crop from which sugar cubes are made, though it is not itself cube-shaped.
explanation.definitionFit: This root crop is refined into the granules pressed into lumps for tea, without itself growing as a lump.

clue.text: Make up topical rhyme about a pound in terms of figures

indicators.note: the rearranged letters wrap around the other piece
to make up is to compose or invent, so the letters are recombined

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for pound, from the Latin libra

explanation.surface: Instructions to compose a topical verse about a sum of money, in numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: Figures here are figures of speech, not numbers; 'Make up' rearranges TOPICAL RHYME and 'about' puts A and L inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Figures of speech include metaphors, so speaking in them means using non-literal language.

clue.text: Security device for Peter workin' at keys

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe
working at a keyboard is typing, and the dropped g of workin' signals the clipped form typin'

explanation.surface: Someone called Peter is busy at the keys, perhaps the typewriter, of some security gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter looks like a man's name but is the safecracker's word for a safe; the apostrophe in workin' tells you to drop the final G of the typing word too.
explanation.definitionFit: A pin with a guarded clasp keeps its point covered, a small device for fastening safely.

clue.text: Coin America disposed of for well below par

definitions.meaning: a former American ten-dollar gold coin, no longer minted
in golf, a hole completed two strokes under par

explanation.surface: A coin that America got rid of is worth far less than face value.
explanation.walkthrough: The US gold ten-dollar piece bore this name and was withdrawn; golfers use the same word for two under par on a hole.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses come from the bird: an American gold coin stamped with it, and golf's score two strokes under par.

clue.text: Orpington for example, always dividing political sides

indicators.note: one word splits the other here, sitting between the two political sides

parts.note: left and right, abbreviated L and R
aye is a poetic word for always, as in for ever and aye

explanation.surface: An Orpington politician is always caught between the left and the right.
explanation.walkthrough: Orpington is a London suburb, which makes it look political, but it is also a British breed of chicken, kept for its eggs.
explanation.definitionFit: Orpingtons are a breed of hen, and a hen kept for eggs is called by the farmer's term for an egg producer.

clue.text: No end to Hibernian rainbow?

indicators.note: the final letter of the word for Hibernian is cut off, leaving it without its end

parts.note: Hibernia is the Latin name for Ireland, so Hibernian means Irish

explanation.surface: An Irish rainbow that goes on forever, never reaching its end.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as a stretch: the Greek goddess of the rainbow carries this name, and the eye's coloured ring is named after her.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the rainbow was personified as the messenger goddess, and the word in Greek means rainbow itself.

clue.text: Region of nameless battleground

indicators.note: without a name means losing N, the standard abbreviation for name

parts.note: an arena is a place of combat or contest

explanation.surface: A region known for an unnamed battlefield.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nameless' reads as an adjective for the battleground but splits as name (N) plus less, a removal.
explanation.definitionFit: A zone or district of land is a direct synonym, as in a residential district.

clue.text: The clever men at Oxford were this, said Grahame

definitions.text: The clever men at Oxford were this, said Grahame

parts.words: The clever men at Oxford were this, said Grahame
parts.note: Kenneth Grahame's Toad sings that the clever men at Oxford know all that there is to be known

explanation.surface: An author recalls how the Oxford dons struck him.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Wind in the Willows Toad boasts: 'The clever men at Oxford / Know all that there is to be knowed', but none knows half as much as he.
explanation.definitionFit: Knowing all that there is to be known is the meaning of all-knowing.

clue.text: This is for tricky places, beginning laparotomy

definitions.text: This is for tricky places, beginning laparotomy

indicators.note: tricky suggests something intricate or twisted, so the word places is rearranged
only the opening letter of laparotomy is taken

explanation.surface: A surgeon describes the instrument needed for awkward spots at the start of an abdominal operation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tricky' rearranges PLACES into SCALPE, and 'beginning' takes the L of laparotomy, an abdominal incision; the whole clue then describes the surgeon's blade.
explanation.definitionFit: A surgeon's small sharp knife is what opens an abdominal incision and works in delicate spots.

clue.text: Second mowing ordered at the farm

indicators.note: ordered means arranged anew, so these letters are put into a different order

explanation.surface: A second cutting of grass is scheduled at the farm.
explanation.walkthrough: The original farming sense is a second crop of grass mown after the first; the modern sense of consequences grew from it.
explanation.definitionFit: Math is an old word for a mowing, so the later crop of grass cut after the first is its literal meaning.

clue.text: Palace walk that started with lane, capitally?

definitions.text: Palace walk that started with lane, capitally?

parts.words: Palace walk that started with lane, capitally?
parts.note: a London district naming the archbishop's palace and a famous Cockney dance popularised by the actor Lupino Lane in the capital

explanation.surface: A stroll by a palace that began down a little lane in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Lane is not a road but Lupino Lane, the comedian who launched the dance song 'The Lambeth Walk' in the 1937 musical Me and My Girl; the district's palace is the Archbishop of Canterbury's London home.
explanation.definitionFit: This south London borough houses the archbishop's palace and gave its name to the Cockney dance of the musical stage.

clue.text: Having written music, gesture of approval goes round gallery

indicators.note: one word surrounds the other, the nod encircling the gallery

parts.note: a nod of the head signals agreement
the Tate is the famous London art gallery

explanation.surface: A composer finishes a score and gets a nod of approval at the gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is London's national gallery of British and modern art.
explanation.definitionFit: Setting down a tune in written symbols is a past participle, so 'having written music' describes it, as in a scored piece.

clue.text: Painful exclamation by girl Sally?

parts.note: a deb, short for debutante, is a young society girl
ouch is the cry of pain

explanation.surface: Sally the girl cries out in pain.
explanation.walkthrough: Sally looks like the girl's name, but as a verb it means to rush out, as troops sally from a fort.
explanation.definitionFit: To emerge from a narrow place into open ground, as troops do in a sortie, is the military sense.

clue.text: Dog star?

definitions.meaning: a gun dog breed that stands rigid indicating game
either of the two stars of the Plough that line up toward the Pole Star

explanation.surface: Sirius, the dog star, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: Read together the words suggest Sirius, the Dog Star; split apart they give a gun dog and one of the two stars in the Plough that guide the eye to the Pole Star.
explanation.definitionFit: A gun dog that indicates game, and two stars of the Plough that indicate the north star, both share one name.

clue.text: First class idiot has' record turned over — what a bloomer!

indicators.note: everything before is flipped, so the whole run of pieces reads backwards

parts.note: A1 means first class, with the 1 written as I
a nut is a crazy person
EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A first-class fool turns over his record, and makes a terrible blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned over' reverses AINUTEP. A bloomer is a blunder, but here it is anything that blooms, a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: A garden flower in many colours, and anything that blooms can be jokingly called a bloomer.

clue.text: Carriage left bearing wine

definitions.meaning: the way one holds oneself, deportment or bearing
the left-hand side of a ship facing forward

explanation.surface: A carriage leaves, carrying a load of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings run in a row: carriage in the sense of bearing, the nautical word for left, and Portuguese fortified wine; bearing is a link that glosses the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Deportment, a ship's left side and a fortified Douro wine all share one short word.

clue.text: Border set-back for euphonium

indicators.note: set back here means turned backwards, so the instrument's name runs in reverse

parts.note: the euphonium is a small tenor tuba, so tuba stands for it

explanation.surface: A border is a setback for a euphonium player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set-back' looks like a noun meaning a reverse of fortune but is the reversal signal; the euphonium is the brass family's tenor tuba.
explanation.definitionFit: To border is to lie adjacent, touching at an edge, which is the verb's meaning.

clue.text: Dicey-looking apprentice in charge

parts.note: a cub is a novice or trainee, as in cub reporter

explanation.surface: A trainee left in charge looks a risky bet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicey' means risky in the surface, but here it means shaped like dice.
explanation.definitionFit: Dice are cubes, so looking like a die means having the shape of a cube.

clue.text: Split down the middle provided the offer is external

indicators.note: the offer sits outside, holding the other piece within

parts.note: a bid is an offer of a price
if means provided that

explanation.surface: A deal is split down the middle, provided the offer comes from outside.
explanation.walkthrough: Botanists use the word for a leaf or petal cleft in two.
explanation.definitionFit: Biology uses this word for anything cleft in two parts, as a forked tongue or divided leaf.

clue.text: See the combined gathering

definitions.meaning: joining the two words see and the gives seethe, to bubble furiously
a gathering is an abscess or swelling full of pus

explanation.surface: Look at the assembled crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: Run 'See the' together and you get SEETHE, which means to bubble as water does when heated; a gathering is an old word for a pus-filled swelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Seething liquid bubbles hot, and a pus-filled swelling on the skin shares the same name.

clue.text: One mile past — butterfly for one can go no further

definitions.text: butterfly for one can go no further

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
ago means in the past

explanation.surface: Past the one-mile mark, a butterfly runs out of steam.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads as a tired runner but describes an insect's final, adult stage, beyond which it develops no further.
explanation.definitionFit: The adult winged stage is the last of an insect's metamorphosis, so a butterfly reaches it and develops no more.

clue.text: A French word for tin is not 'necessary

parts.note: un is French for a
both tin and 'the needful' are slang for money

explanation.surface: A French word meaning tin is apparently not required.
explanation.walkthrough: Tin and 'the needful' are both old British slang for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Something required is needful, so its negated form means superfluous or dispensable.

clue.text: In an apathetic way he hardly felt a reform

indicators.note: reform means to form again, so these letters are rebuilt in a different order

explanation.surface: Someone who barely felt a reform reacts with indifference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reform' rearranges HEHARDLYFELTA, and the fodder itself reads as lukewarm feeling.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something without enthusiasm or commitment is acting with only partial heart.
